title: Kevin Mansfield PhD FSLL
text:
I am a researcher and educator in light and lighting since the late 1970’s with a particular emphasis on the built environment. I was the Course Director for many years of the MSc Light and Lighting offered at UCL’s Bartlett Faculty of the Built Environment which has been responsible for a generation of graduates in the multidisciplinary consultancies, the independent lighting design houses and the lighting companies both here in the UK and internationally. I have also supervised many doctoral students in lighting. I am a Fellow of the Society of Light and Lighting.
Please feel free to explore, this, my small corner of the web.

title: Projects
text:
The Daylighting of the Stave Church of Borgund, Norway
I have always been intrigued by descriptions in the art history literature of the atmospheric effects of daylighting in sacred buildings. For example, Norberg-Schulz in his book Nightlands: Nordic Building describes the interior of a stave church thus

the weak light is split by roof work and sinks like a dim atmosphere into the room.


Open Access preprint
The stave church of Borgund, Norway |  (www.wondermondo.com/Norway.htm [CC BY-SA 2.0])
In a study of the daylighting of the stave church of Borgund in Norway, I claim that the true spirit of Nordic lighting is to be found in the original medieval church and attempt to characterise the quality of daylighting that was achieved. The work was presented at the Nordic Lighting Conference 2012 and can be found here.
Towards the end of the paper I consider how modes of appearance concepts may assist interpretation of the field of view—concepts which I consider undervalued in assessment of daylighting quality in interiors.

title: Field utilisation of a light dosimeter
text:
There is intense interest within the lighting community in the wide-ranging biological responses to light together with the view that proper exposure to daylight is vital for our health and well-being. An advanced light dosimeter, developed by Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts (LUASA), has the potential to accurately capture daylight availability experienced by workplace occupants and demonstrate whether contemporary buildings provide light of the appropriate intensity, duration and spectral composition.



Light Dosimeter


The light dosimeter developed by LUASA
Could the novel light dosimeter be deployed in the field in the UK? Participants in architecturally distinct workplace environments could monitor their ‘light dose’ for a week. Depending on the workplace context being different during this pandemic, it may be better to opt for ‘hybrid’ workplaces combining both traditional office and home working. Once the data is collected, a lighting metric (𝜶-opic daylight equivalent illuminance), recommended by the Commission Internationale de l’Eclairage (CIE) for good quality lighting, could be computed.
The immediate outcome of this type of project would be unique evidence-based data to describe the ‘light dose’ experienced in a variety of distinct workplace architectural environments. We could use these data to confirm proposed metrics in lighting quality and/or propose new ones and we could use these findings to contribute to the WELL building standard (International WELL Building Institute) and the Society of Light and Lighting’s (SLL) Codes and Guidance documents. Such a novel and wearable sensor for conducting real world research could inform the design of healthy buildings in the longer term.
Details of the light dosimeter can be found at be found https://light-dosimeter.ch/

title: Unification in Mathematics
text:
Very struck by a passage in W. W. Sawyer’s Prelude to Mathematics (dating from 1955) concerning ‘unification’ in mathematics:

…hundreds of papers are written, each clarifying one facet of the truth; the subject is growing. … It then ceases to be necessary to read the hundreds of separate contributions… The variegated results are welded together into a single doctrine… The new methods having become common property, new problems are found which they are insufficient to solve…new papers are published; expansion begins again. There always is, there always will be something to learn, something to conquer.

title: Publications
text:
The perplexities of lighting education
My thoughts about lighting education recently published as an opinion piece in Lighting Research and Technology (Volume 49 No 2 (2017)).

We have a problem over how to educate future lighting designers and practitioners. This is a divergent problem, in the sense coined by E. F. Schumacher in his book A Guide for the Perplexed, in that some say that those who have knowledge and experience should teach and those who lack knowledge and experience should learn. In contrast, others say that we should provide an environment where the student is allowed the freedom to flourish. Schumacher suggests that we should transcend these opposites by actually caring about the student.
I have spent most of my professional life addressing this question and have seen many changes in architectural and urban design as well as transformative developments in light sources and lighting controls. Here I outline what I feel to be the essential components of a rich lighting education and would like to warmly acknowledge Robert Sedgewick of Princeton University whose writings on the future educational landscape have informed my thoughts.
The problem is that we need light to live. Depending on how we deliver lighting we can either enhance or destroy architectural intent; we can increase the legibility of our cities or generate insecure, threatening environments. We can reveal or distort the nature and modelling of faces, surfaces and objects. These are complex problems that require the lighting scholar to draw from many different disciplines—the natural sciences, engineering, the social sciences, architectural and urban design as well as photometry and colorimetry.
There are three educational abstractions that are needed for the education of the lighting designer or practitioner. We need textbooks for use by students to learn and study. We need lighting courses that encourage communities of students to learn together. We need web content for use by students to explore and interact with lighting topics. For textbooks we have excellent offerings in the areas of human factors, lighting calculations and the overall design of lighting. But there seem to be gaps regarding good textbooks on solid state lighting, daylighting prediction and visualisation, light and health and lighting design strategies at the urban scale. Digital technologies now give us the opportunity to deliver web content such as video, animations and lighting demonstrations forming a living online document supporting and extending the textbooks available. They also give the facility to deliver reproducible research—transparent and freely available lighting design computations and daylight modelling processes whose details and intent are currently hidden. And our lighting courses need to deliver lighting material, engage with students and, importantly, provide validation of their learning. Much of this can be delivered in lectures, seminars, workshops and project briefings with peer review. And there must be a research component—perhaps a dissertation or a technical report, design document or feasibility study similar to outputs generated by consultants in the real world.
To become a fully rounded lighting professional takes time but with the potential of light to make such an impact on our lives, surely we must rise to the challenge.

title: Dr Kevin Mansfield FSLL
text:
Welcome

I have spent most of my working life researching and teaching light and lighting in the built environment.
My research interests span architectural lighting, the human response to lighting and the impact of lighting at urban, architectural and object scales.
On this website, you will find a selection of my published works, including scholarly articles, and news and updates on my current research projects.




Contact
Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions or would like to discuss potential projects.
